title: 10 Wonderkids Who Failed to Live Up to the Hype
subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Barnaby Lane7:00 PM ESTRenato Sanches had so much potential. / Athena Pictures/Getty ImagesFew things are more exciting than watching a young talent burst onto the scene, take the world by storm and seemingly announce the arrival of the next global superstar.

For some, the hype becomes reality. Lionel Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo and Neymar all went on to fulfill their extraordinary potential. Lamine Yamal and Jude Bellingham are doing the same. For countless others, however, the story played out rather differently. Some faded into obscurity, while others spent their careers chasing the heights they were once tipped to reach.
Being labelled a wonderkid can be both a blessing and a curse. The expectations, pressure and constant scrutiny can become overwhelming, and not everyone is equipped to handle them.
These 10 players are among the most striking examples of soccer’s biggest teenage sensations who, for one reason or another, never quite lived up to the hype.

Rodwell isn’t popular in Sunderland. / Michael Regan/Getty ImagesTwo promising seasons as a youngster at Everton were enough to convince Manchester City to splash out on Jack Rodwell in 2012. But the England midfielder struggled to make an impression at the Etihad, managing just a handful of appearances before joining Sunderland on a five-year deal in 2014.What followed was a nightmare for the Black Cats. Plagued by injuries, Rodwell managed fewer than 45 league starts across more than three seasons, all while reportedly collecting £70,000 a week in wages. As Sunderland spiraled from established Premier League club to League One strugglers, his hefty contract became a major financial burden, with Rodwell determined to see out his lucrative deal despite his limited involvement on the pitch.Unsurprisingly, he didn’t exactly leave Wearside with a glowing reputation, spending much of the remainder of his career drifting between clubs and winding down his playing days in Australia.

Pato struggled with injuries. / Alberto Lingria/AFP/Getty ImagesCalling Alexandre Pato a flop is excessive. He made more than 150 appearances for AC Milan, scored over 50 goals and lifted a Serie A title during his time at San Siro.But such was the sheer scale of his talent that, somehow, it still felt like an underachievement.Bursting onto the scene as a teenager in one of Milan’s most iconic squads, Pato appeared to have everything needed to become one of world soccer’s very best. Blessed with blistering pace, effortless flair, a natural eye for goal and the fearlessness of youth, he looked destined for superstardom. His stunning solo goal after just 24 seconds against Barcelona in the 2011 Champions League was a perfect illustration of what he could produce.But injuries soon began to take their toll. Recurring fitness problems disrupted his rhythm, inconsistency crept into his performances and the extraordinary potential that once surrounded him slowly began to fade.The 2009 Golden Boy winner was back in Brazil by 2013, and, aside from an unexpected loan spell at Chelsea in 2016, he never came close to rediscovering the form that had made him one of soccer’s most exciting prospects between 2007 and 2009.

Federico Macheda burst onto the scene. / Matthew Peters/Manchester United/Getty ImagesFederico Macheda’s Manchester United debut could hardly have gone any better.The 17-year-old Italian seemingly appeared out of nowhere, announcing himself to the world with a sensational last-minute winner against Aston Villa that helped keep United’s Premier League title charge on track. Overnight, he was the talk of English soccer and looked destined for a glittering future at Old Trafford.Unfortunately, that was pretty much as good as it got.Macheda managed just four more goals in a United shirt, instead becoming something of a loan specialist. Between 2011 and 2014, he was shipped out five times, bouncing between Italy, Germany and the lower reaches of English soccer in search of the form that had initially made him such an exciting prospect.A respectable loan spell at Birmingham City in the Championship, followed by a more productive stint at Greek side Panathinaikos, offered glimpses of his ability. But it soon became apparent that Macheda’s future lay some distance from the elite level many had once predicted for him.

Drenthe didn’t cut it at soccer or rapping. / Queimadelos Alonso/Getty ImagesFew players have experienced quite such a rapid fall from grace as Royston Drenthe.Real Madrid came calling when the Dutchman was just 20, following a breakout season with Feyenoord that had put some of Europe’s biggest clubs on alert. Expectations were high, but things quickly unravelled. Loan spells at Hércules and Everton followed, neither of which produced much to shout about, before he eventually left the Bernabéu as a free agent.What followed was a truly nomadic career, taking him everywhere from Russia and Turkey to the UAE, with further stops in England, Spain and the Netherlands. His performances rarely made headlines, but his colorful life away from the pitch certainly did.Drenthe tried his hand at rap, launched his own fashion brand before subsequently going bankrupt and attracted plenty of tabloid attention for his personal life, including relationships with multiple women and fathering eight children with eight different partners.

John Bostock was tipped to reach the very top.  / Victor Fraile/Corbis/etty ImagesJohn Bostock broke through at Crystal Palace at the age of 15 and his name was quickly circulating in gossip columns as Real Madrid, Barcelona and Liverpool circled.Ultimately, it was Tottenham Hotspur who picked up Bostock after going through a tribunal—Palace furious with how the transfer and the conduct of the player and his father. Nevertheless, big things were expected of the 6'2" playmaker, but it became apparent quite quickly that his projected rise to superstardom wasn’t going to happen.A series of lower league loan spells did little to help Bostock’s cause, and he left Spurs five years after joining having failed to make a single Premier League appearance. His next landing spot was in Belgium, where he briefly flirted with a return to prominence after a decent two-year spell at OH Leuven.Subsequent moves to Türkiye and France didn’t go well, and the only real stability of Bostock’s career came when he plummeted down the English pyramid with stints at Doncaster Rovers, Notts County and Solihull Moors.“In hindsight, I should have stayed [at Palace],” Bostock later mused.

Sanches flopped at Bayern. / Bongarts/Getty ImagesRenato Sanches was once one of Europe’s most exciting young talents, but his big-money move from Benfica to Bayern Munich proved a turning point for all the wrong reasons.Bayern splashed €35 million on the Portuguese midfielder in 2016, making him the fourth-most expensive signing in the club’s history at the time. But despite arriving with enormous expectations, Sanches struggled for opportunities, managing just one full 90 minutes in the Bundesliga during his debut season and failing to register a single goal or assist.A loan to Swansea City followed, where he famously passed the ball straight into an advertising hoarding, before Bayern eventually sold him to Lille in 2019.Things hardly improved thereafter. Sanches became a perennial loanee, struggling to make an impression during subsequent spells in Italy, back in Portugal and in Greece.

Bojan was supposed to be Messi’s heir. / Jasper Juinen/Getty ImagesThere have been plenty of players branded as the next Lionel Messi over the years. Bojan Krkić was the first.After breaking a record previously held by Messi to become Barcelona’s youngest-ever debutant, the Spaniard looked destined to become the club’s next generational superstar. A tricky, technically gifted forward blessed with flair and natural goalscoring instincts, Bojan initially looked every bit the wonderkid Barcelona believed they had. But as his early promise began to fade around 2011, loan spells failed to reignite his career, and even a return to Camp Nou couldn’t get him back on track.By 2014, Barcelona had moved on, and Bojan found himself at Stoke City in the Premier League. It was a far cry from the heights once predicted for him.Spells in the United States and Japan followed before he eventually called time on his playing career in 2023 with just one senior cap for Spain to his name.

Hachim Mastour was supposed to take the world by storm. / Fabio Ionà/Corbis/Getty ImagesHachim Mastour had all of Europe’s biggest clubs purring as a teenager, with Barcelona, Juventus, Real Madrid, Inter and Manchester City all reportedly targeting him. But the 14-year-old Moroccan-Italian opted to join AC Milan in 2012.A YouTube sensation, Mastour was dubbed the next Neymar thanks to his dazzling skills, outrageous tricks and seemingly limitless potential. Things got off to a promising start, too, with the teenager making it into Milan’s first-team setup before a two-year loan spell at Málaga appeared to offer the perfect next step.But Mastour never managed to secure consistent first-team soccer during his formative years, and his development gradually ground to a halt. After slipping down the Italian pyramid with spells in Serie B and Serie C, he eventually joined Moroccan second-tier side Renaissance Zemamra in 2022  before returning to Italy to play Serie D soccer.

Ravel Morrison was so , so talented. / Martin Rickett/PA Images/Getty ImagesAsk almost any former Manchester United player who watched Ravel Morrison as a youngster, and they’ll tell you the same thing: his talent was extraordinary. Even Sir Alex Ferguson once described him as the “most talented player” he’d ever worked with.But while his ability was never in question, his troubles away from the pitch would ultimately prevent him from fulfilling his enormous potential.Morrison’s early career was plagued by disciplinary issues and run-ins with the law, including convictions for witness intimidation and criminal damage, assault charges (from which he was later cleared), and an FA fine for a homophobic tweet. Questions over his professionalism also followed him, with managers such as Sam Allardyce highlighting his struggles with timekeeping, training commitments and maintaining the discipline required of a full-time professional.Ultimately, Morrison became a heartbreaking example of talent alone not being enough. Ferguson believed his difficult upbringing and personal struggles played a significant role in preventing him from reaching the extraordinary heights his ability promised.“Sadly, there are examples of players who have similar backgrounds to [Ryan] Giggs or Cristiano Ronaldo, who, despite enormous talent, just aren’t emotionally or mentally strong enough to overcome the hurts of their childhood and their inner demons,” Ferguson said.“Ravel Morrison might be the saddest case.”

Adu never lived up to the hype. / Gail Oskin/MLSNETImagesFreddy Adu was supposed to change the trajectory of US soccer forever.Few teenagers have ever arrived with quite so much hype. After signing a professional contract in the United States at just 14, Adu burst onto the scene with D.C. United, quickly becoming one of the most talked-about young talents in world soccer. The comparisons were inevitable: a young Pelé, destined for greatness.But the fairytale failed to materialize.Fast-forward a few years, and the once-touted wonderkid had become a footballing nomad, perpetually moving from one loan spell to the next. Adu would go on to represent 15 clubs across nine different countries, with career stops ranging from Brazil to Finland.His professional journey finally came to an end in 2021, after his contract was terminated by Swedish side Österlen FF. For a player once tipped to revolutionize American soccer, it was a remarkably sobering conclusion.
